sections.COMMENTS:
The Dinarides are a wide NW-SE fold-and-thrust belt stretching from southwestern Slovenia to Montenegro along the Adriatic coast of Croatia and inland. The Dinarides formed as a consequence of subduction and collision processes in the border zone between Europe and Adria tectonic plates. Adria acted, and is still acting, as an indenter moving roughly towards stable Europe and causing the Meso-Cenozoic carbonate rocks of the Dinaric platform to over-ride onto the Adriatic lithosphere (e.g. Aljinovic et al., 1990; Prelogovic et al., 1995; Herak, 1999). The most prominent structures of the Dinarides are NW-SE oriented thrust faults (Mamuzic, 1975; Ivanovic et al., 1976; Herak, 1991, 1999). Present day tectonic rates are mostly obtained from GPS campaigns and display general NNE-SSW to NE-SW trends, with values of 2-2.5 mm/yr in northern Dalmatia (Grenerczy et al., 2005) and 4-4.5 mm/yr in central and southern Dinarides (Grenerczy et al., 2005; Bennett et al., 2008; Devoti et al., 2008).
Within the Dinarides the seismicity is distributed along the entire length of the belt. Data on both instrumental and historical seismicity show earthquake activity across the entire width of the thrust belt. Available focal mechanism solutions (Herak et al., 1995; Vannucci et al., 2004) and structural geological data show, that at its NW end the seismic deformation is dominated by right-lateral movement on NW-SE strike-slip faults. In the central and southern part of the belt, both in the off-shore and coastal parts, thrusting is the prevailing mode of seismic deformation whereas in the inner parts of the belt the fault planes are steeper and show more complex kinematics with reverse, strike-slip and oblique movements. Active processes in this region are mainly driven by NE oriented compression, documented from maximum compressive axis orientation of focal mechanisms (Anderson and Jackson, 1987; Pondrelli et al., 2006) and from long-term geological evidence (Prelogovic et al., 2003).
This Source is a NW-SE oriented offshore thrust fault positioned in the central part of the Adriatic Sea and represents one of the most external thrust fronts of the Dinaric side of Adria. We assign the Jana-1 fault to the Dinaric thrust front with the dip-direction towards NE, but alternative interpretations which group the fault to the Apennine thrust belt with prevailing dip direction towards SW also exist (e.g. Scrocca et al., 2006). The ambiguity in the interpretation is in large part due to the presence of salt dipirism, masking the tectonic input of the deformation and lowering the quality of reflection on seismic profiles.
We set the depth interval of the source taking into account data on regional structural setting and the location of earthquakes (Herak et al., 1995).
The strongest earthquake associated with this Source is the 5 September 1920 event reaching a magnitude value Ma 5.0 (CPTI04). Other strong seismic events include the Ml 4.9 earthquake of 27 March 2003 (CMT Harvard), the 25 May 1951 Ma 4.8 event (CPTI04), as well as the 1986 seismic sequence with the largest event occurred on 26 January with magnitude Mw 4.4 (Pondrelli et al., 2006).
We set the strike dip and rake of the source in accordance with seismic profiling and geological data (Ridente and Trincardi, 2006; Geletti et al., 2008) together with fault plane solutions of recent earthquakes from Pondrelli et al. (2006). We estimated the slip rate on the basis of horizontal velocities obtained by GPS campaigns (Caporali et al., 2009) and considering geometric characteristics of the fault.

pictures.t: Structural and seismicity map of central Adriatic
pictures.c: Structural map of the active faults in the central Adriatic. The location and geometry of the Palagruza fault is shown together with the focal mechanism solution for the strongest instrumentally recorded earthquake associated with it (from Ridente and Trincardi, [2006]).

pictures.t: Detail of seismic profile data through the Central Adriatic
pictures.c: Results of seismic imaging crossing Jana-1 fault (Geletti et al, 2008). Seismic images demonstrate the presence of a diapir body and fault planes, while a more detailed Chirp dataset proves a fault trace deforming the sea-floor.

pictures.c: Interpreted regional seismic reflection profiles (no. 6 and 7) straddling the width of the central Adriatic basin and the adjacent Northern Apennines (to the west) and Dinarides (to the east) (modified, from Fantoni and Franciosi [2009]).
